questions_and_answers.question_text: How is cóng usually used in modern Chinese?
What is the difference in meaning between wàng and dào?
How else may wàng be pronounced?
How many prepositional verb phrases occur before the main verb in this sentence?
Write the Chinese for "From here you go to the left."
Is cóng often used as a full verb?

answers.answer_text: No — unlike the other prepositional verbs, it is only rarely used as a full verb in modern Chinese.
"Towards" or "in the direction of" — without implying arrival.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which word implies eventual arrival at a destination?
Give the Chinese words for "left" and "right."

articles.text:
4. C: Cóng zhèli wàng zuǒ zǒu.       From here you go to the left.

Notes on No. 4

Cóng, "from": Unlike the other prepositional verbs you have learned, cóng is only rarely used as a full verb in modern Chinese. Most frequently, it is used prepositionally.

Wàng, "to," "towards": The prepositional verbs wàng and dào may both be translated as "to." Wàng, however, means simply "towards" or "in the direction of," while dào implies eventual arrival at a destination. Wàng may also be pronounced wǎng.

Notice that two prepositional verb phrases occur before the main verb.

PREPOSITIONAL VERB AND NOUN  |  PREPOSITIONAL VERB AND NOUN  |  MAIN VERB
cóng zhèli                   |  wàng zuǒ                      |  zǒu
